interviewQuestions.question: A cross-platform app is janky on a specific screen. Walk through how you'd actually diagnose it, layer by layer.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by naming the specific shape of the jank rather than treating it as one generic problem — is it during a gesture (points to high-frequency boundary crossings), a long list scroll (points to virtualization), first load of a screen with images (points to decode cost), or app startup (points to script parsing or shader compilation)? That framing already narrows where to look before opening any profiler.

Then I'd start at the framework level: React DevTools Profiler or Flutter DevTools' rebuild tracking, to see whether the JS/Dart-side logic is doing more work than it should — an unmemoized component re-rendering every frame, a widget rebuilding a large subtree unnecessarily. If that layer is clean but the jank persists, I'd drop to a native profiler — Xcode Instruments or Android Profiler — to check whether the cost is actually happening in native layout, painting, or GPU work below what the framework tool instruments.

For React Native specifically, I'd also check Flipper or a Perfetto trace for bridge/JSI traffic volume during the janky interaction — a spike in message frequency correlated with the gesture is a strong signal the boundary itself, not either side's logic, is the bottleneck.

Only once I've localized the actual layer would I apply a fix — batching cross-boundary calls, virtualizing a list, moving an interaction to a natively-driven animation library, or optimizing native image decoding — because the fix differs completely depending on which layer is actually responsible.

**Testing:** whether you profile methodically layer-by-layer instead of guessing at a fix from the symptom alone.

interviewQuestions.question: You need to expose a native biometric authentication API to your cross-platform app's JavaScript or Dart code. Walk through building this, and what you'd watch for.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd write a thin native module per platform — Swift wrapping `LocalAuthentication` on iOS, Kotlin wrapping `BiometricPrompt` on Android — each exposing a narrow, purpose-built interface: something like `authenticate(reason: String) -> Promise<Bool>`, not a broad mirror of the entire native API surface. The JS/Dart side then just calls an async function; the platform-specific complexity stays entirely on the native side where it belongs.

What I'd watch for specifically: biometric APIs have real platform differences in error handling — iOS distinguishes several failure reasons (not enrolled, locked out, user cancelled) and Android's equivalents don't map 1:1 — so I'd design the JS-facing error contract deliberately rather than just passing native error codes through unexamined, since the app's UI needs to handle 'no biometrics enrolled' differently from 'user cancelled' regardless of platform.

I'd hold both platform implementations to the same testing bar from the start — write the test plan (success, denial, lockout, not-enrolled, cancelled-mid-flow) before implementing either platform, not iOS-first with Android as an afterthought, since that asymmetry is exactly how a module ends up working well on one platform and crashing or misbehaving on the other.

Finally, I'd keep the actual credential/biometric handling entirely on the native side — never pass anything sensitive back across the bridge/channel beyond a plain success/failure result, since the boundary itself isn't the place to route security-sensitive data through unnecessarily.

**Testing:** whether you design the interface deliberately and hold both platforms to equal rigor, not just 'wrap the API and ship it.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Design

interviewQuestions.question: Your team wrote a native module for a feature two years ago because the framework didn't support it. The framework has since added native support for that exact feature. Do you migrate away from the custom module?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Probably, but I'd verify rather than assume the framework's version is strictly better. A custom native module, once written, is code the team owns and maintains on two platforms indefinitely — every OS update is a re-testing surface, every framework upgrade is a compatibility check. If the framework's built-in version now covers the same functionality, migrating removes that ongoing maintenance cost entirely, which is a real, compounding win over time.

Before migrating, I'd check for two things: whether the custom module does anything the framework's built-in version doesn't (a specific edge case, a performance characteristic the team tuned for, a behavior difference the product actually depends on), and whether the migration itself is low-risk enough to do without a dedicated testing pass — swapping an authentication or payment-adjacent module, for instance, deserves the same rigor as the original implementation did, not a rushed swap.

If the custom module has accumulated genuine value beyond what the framework offers, I'd keep it and document explicitly why, so the next engineer doesn't propose the same 'just use the built-in version' migration without that context. If it's a clean superset, I'd migrate and treat the maintenance-cost reduction as the actual win, not just a code-cleanliness exercise.

**Testing:** whether you think about migration as a cost-benefit decision with real verification, not a reflexive 'newer is better' move.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: A performance fix for a janky list feels significantly smoother on your development iPhone. How confident are you that it actually fixed the problem for real users, and what would you do before declaring it done?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Not very confident from that evidence alone, and I wouldn't declare it done yet. A development device is almost always faster and less loaded than the median real device in production — no background apps competing for CPU, often a newer chipset, and none of the thermal throttling a phone sees after twenty minutes of real use. 'Feels smoother on my dev phone' is a weak signal for whether the fix actually moves the needle for the users experiencing the original complaint.

Before calling it done, I'd want a concrete before-and-after metric captured from real usage — frame drop rate or time-to-interactive for the specific screen, instrumented and reported from the app itself, not just observed locally. I'd ship the fix behind a flag or to a percentage of users, compare the metric against the control group, and only roll out fully once the data actually shows improvement across the real device and network distribution the app runs on — including the lower-end devices most likely to have shown the original symptom in the first place.

This matters more for cross-platform apps specifically because the device spread tends to be wider than a native-only app targeting, say, only recent iPhones — an app running on a five-year-old budget Android device and a current-generation iPhone can show wildly different results for the same code change.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish 'feels better to me' from 'measurably better for real users,' which is the actual senior-level discipline here.
